extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of the State of New York and readers interested in U.S. constitutional design (general public, 1788-era political readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from The Federalist Papers (Nos. 35–37) arguing for a general federal power of taxation, concurrent jurisdiction with the states, and the sufficiency of representative bodies; aimed to persuade New York readers about adopting the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction in taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: "A CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent jurisdiction reconciles an indefinite federal power of taxation with an adequate, independent power in the States to provide for their own necessities; it avoids sacrificing the Union's interests to individual States. (Explained as preferable to exclusive federal control or complete subordination of states.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restricting federal taxation to particular objects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jurisdiction of the national government in the article of revenue should be restricted to particular objects, it would naturally occasion an undue proportion of the public burdens to fall upon those objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting federal revenue to specific sources (e.g., imports) leads to oppression of particular industries, smuggling, monopolies for manufacturing classes, and unequal tax distribution among states and citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import duties should be a national common stock
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is far more equitable that the duties on imports should go into a common stock, than that they should redound to the exclusive benefit of the importing States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because consumers (not only merchants) ultimately bear duties variably, import duties should fund national needs rather than benefit particular states to prevent interstate inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify national revenue sources beyond imposts
rubrics_metrics.description: Confinement of the national revenues to this species of imposts would be attended with inequality... between the manufacturing and the non-manufacturing States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on import duties disadvantages non-importing/manufacturing states; recourse to excises and other internal taxes is necessary to align contributions with states' abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue interest guards against excessive duties (but only if alternatives exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of the revenue itself would be a sufficient guard against such an extreme. I readily admit that this would be the case, as long as other resources were open; but if the avenues to them were closed, HOPE, stimulated by necessity, would beget experiments...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government's self-interest in stable revenue limits harmful tax excesses—but this safeguard weakens if revenue options are artificially constrained, which can lead to coercive or excessive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies need not include a member per occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of an actual representation of all classes of the people, by persons of each class, is altogether visionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent explicit constitutional provision for occupational quotas, voters will choose representatives (often merchants, landholders, learned professions) who in practice represent wider class interests; attempting to engineer occupational representation is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural representation via allied interests (merchants as representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics and manufacturers will always be inclined, with few exceptions, to give their votes to merchants... Many of them... are immediately connected with the operations of commerce. They know that the merchant is their natural patron and friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral behavior will create de facto representation of various productive classes through allied, better-equipped representatives rather than direct occupational delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and ability matter more than exact local representation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no part of the administration of government that requires extensive information and a thorough knowledge of the principles of political economy, so much as the business of taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those charged with taxation should possess broad knowledge of the nation's resources and habits; capable, informed legislators will better avoid oppressive expedients than purely locally representative—but less informed—actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: National legislature can and should use state systems for local execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The national legislature can make use of the SYSTEM OF EACH STATE WITHIN THAT STATE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal laws may adopt state methods of laying and collecting taxes and make use of state officers and regulations to execute federal taxation efficiently and to avoid duplication or public disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of duties, imposts, and excises as a constitutional safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: "All duties, imposts, and excises shall be UNIFORM throughout the United States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitutional requirement of uniformity helps prevent partiality and oppression in federal taxation and limits arbitrary regional disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain taxing power even if rarely used because it strengthens requisitions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the exercise of the power of internal taxation by the Union should be discovered on experiment to be really inconvenient, the federal government may then forbear the use of it, and have recourse to requisitions in its stead... the existence of such a power in the Constitution will have a strong influence in giving efficacy to requisitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the power to tax in the Constitution is justified both because it may be practically useful and because its mere existence strengthens federal bargaining with states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding policy interference through reciprocal forbearance
rubrics_metrics.description: An effectual expedient for this purpose will be, mutually, to abstain from those objects which either side may have first had recourse to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although federal and state laws cannot legally conflict, practical policy clashes can be avoided by mutual abstention from preoccupied revenue objects and by coordinating interests—especially where immediate common interests exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedies against double officers and double taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: In other cases, the probability is that the United States will either wholly abstain from the objects preoccupied for local purposes, or will make use of the State officers and State regulations for collecting the additional imposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using state collection apparatus or abstaining from preoccupied objects are practicable expedients to prevent duplicated bureaucracies and redundant taxation burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency taxing powers (including poll taxes) should be retained
rubrics_metrics.description: I... confess my disapprobation of them [poll taxes]; and though they have prevailed ... I should lament to see them introduced into practice under the national government. But does it follow because there is a power to lay them that they will actually be laid?... There are certain emergencies of nations, in which expedients... become essential to the public weal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even distasteful or seldom-used forms of taxation should remain available constitutionally because rare emergencies may necessitate them; retention of options increases government flexibility in crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population-based apportionment prevents partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be recollected that the proportion of these taxes is not to be left to the discretion of the national legislature, but is to be determined by the numbers of each State, as described in the second section of the first article. An actual census or enumeration of the people must furnish the rule, a circumstance which effectually shuts the door to partiality or oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportioning direct tax burdens by population (census) is presented as a structural safeguard against favoritism or targeted oppression by the national legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect vs direct taxes: differing knowledge and administrative needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The taxes intended to be comprised under the general denomination of internal taxes may be subdivided into those of the DIRECT and those of the INDIRECT kind... the reasoning upon it seems to be confined to the former branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect taxes (duties, excises) require less local detail knowledge and are easier to legislate at the national level; direct taxes (land, houses) require local execution through assessors/commissioners, which can be handled by state personnel under federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient revenue systems minimize burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: It might be demonstrated that the most productive system of finance will always be the least burdensome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design revenue systems for productivity and efficiency to reduce the overall tax burden; careful choice and arrangement of means will tend to protect poorer classes from oppressive impositions.
